what: Build Check Part 1 (ROC Operations Manual §14.2A): every source the Source Register lists for a finding was reopened on 8 October 2026 and each recorded quotation looked for on its page. 'also_says' lists further sentences the checkers confirmed on the same pages.

checks.recorded: "usually in mid-February in the south"
checks.page_wording: Roses can be pruned during late winter when growth is just resuming, usually in mid-February in the south, but in northern and colder areas wait until March.
checks.note: Main pruning of modern bush roses. 'The south' stated without a boundary; UK, no other place stated. Supports mid-February for the south/milder band. No date on page.

checks.recorded: "but in northern and colder areas wait until March."
checks.page_wording: ...but in northern and colder areas wait until March.
checks.note: Supports March for northern and colder areas (UK, no place stated beyond 'northern and colder'). Page says 'March' only, not 'mid to late March', so the 'mid to late' wording of the finding is not supported.

checks.recorded: "Roses can be pruned during late winter when growth is just resuming"
checks.page_wording: Roses can be pruned during late winter when growth is just resuming
checks.note: Ties pruning to growth just resuming, a plant signal, alongside months. Only one signal; no mention of buds, dormancy or frost-free day. Main pruning, UK, no place stated.

checks.recorded: "usually in mid-February in the south, but in northern and colder areas wait until March."
checks.page_wording: usually in mid-February in the south, but in northern and colder areas wait until March.
checks.note: Shows two broad bands (south; northern and colder areas) and gives no boundary. The 'none states a boundary' part concerns all sources; this page alone is consistent with it.

checks.recorded: "Late winter (February or March) is often a good time for pruning roses"
checks.page_wording: Late winter (February or March) is often a good time for pruning roses
checks.note: Supports February to March for pruning roses. UK, no place stated. Sentence says 'often', and is about roses generally, not specifically established bush roses; 'early spring' part not stated in this sentence.

also_says.quote: Feed all pruned roses with a general purpose or rose fertiliser in spring
also_says.note: Feeding after pruning, spring, no month; UK, no place stated. Single-fetch, not re-confirmed.

checks.recorded: "in March/April before flowering"
checks.page_wording: in March/April before flowering
checks.note: First feed of roses, March/April, UK no place stated. Supports 'most often March or April' but not the 'late February' start.

checks.recorded: "in mid-summer after the first flush of flowers (especially for repeat-flowering types)"
checks.page_wording: in mid-summer after the first flush of flowers (especially for repeat-flowering types)
checks.note: Further feed in mid-summer after first flush, mainly repeat-flowering types. UK, no place stated.

checks.recorded: "Feed once a fortnight from mid-spring to late summer"
checks.page_wording: Feed once a fortnight from mid-spring to late summer
checks.note: This sentence is about regular fortnightly feeding (context probably container roses; not checked) and gives 'late summer', not 'end of August'. Page gives no end date for feeding. UK, no place stated.

checks.recorded: "you should stop deadheading these plants in mid-summer to give the hips time to form"
checks.page_wording: Some roses produce particularly decorative hips - you should stop deadheading these plants in mid-summer to give the hips time to form
checks.note: Page wording differs trivially in the lead-in. Applies only to roses grown for hips, stop in mid-summer; UK, no place stated. Page gives no 'after the second flush' wording.

checks.recorded: "usually in late autumn or from late winter to early spring, while the plant is not actively growing"
checks.page_wording: usually in late autumn or from late winter to early spring, while the plant is not actively growing
checks.note: Bare-root planting while dormant: late autumn, late winter to early spring. No named months (not October/November/March). UK, no place stated.

checks.recorded: "in March/April before flowering"
checks.page_wording: in March/April before flowering
checks.note: Page gives uniform timing with no regional variation for feeding, deadheading or planting; consistent with no area-specific months. A single page cannot prove the absence in other sources.

contradictions: Page gives no end date for feeding; 'late summer' only.

checks.recorded: "Plant in late autumn at leaf fall, and from late winter to early spring, before growth resumes."
checks.page_wording: Plant in late autumn at leaf fall, and from late winter to early spring, before growth resumes.
checks.note: Bare-root roses, late autumn at leaf fall and late winter to early spring. No months named (not October/November/March). UK, no place stated.

checks.recorded: "Avoid planting in the middle of winter when the ground is frozen."
checks.page_wording: Avoid planting in the middle of winter when the ground is frozen.
checks.note: Bare-root roses; avoid planting when ground frozen in midwinter. UK, no place stated.

checks.recorded: "Plant all year round, provided the ground is neither frozen, nor very dry."
checks.page_wording: Plant all year round, provided the ground is neither frozen, nor very dry.
checks.note: Container-grown roses, any time of year. Page mentions frozen and very dry but not waterlogged. UK, no place stated.

checks.recorded: "remove spent flowers as soon as they look scruffy, whatever the time of year."
checks.page_wording: It's best to remove spent flowers as soon as they look scruffy, whatever the time of year.
checks.note: General deadheading advice for all plants; no place stated. Supports no fixed end month in general, but page names no month to stop for roses and says nothing about autumn or October for roses, so the 'described into autumn and October' part is unsupported here.

checks.recorded: "Move at any time during the dormant season from late October to mid-March"
checks.page_wording: Deciduous plants: Move at any time during the dormant season from late October to mid-March
checks.note: Applies to deciduous shrubs and trees generally; UK, no place stated. Page lists Rosa as resenting root disturbance and tricky to move, so the window is not rose-specific. Supports the late October to mid-March range only.

contradictions: Page names Rosa as resenting root disturbance and tricky to move.

checks.recorded: "Collect and destroy fallen leaves in the autumn, or bury under a layer of mulch."
checks.page_wording: Collect and destroy fallen leaves in the autumn, or bury under a layer of mulch.
checks.note: Clear-up of fallen leaves in autumn, for black spot control; UK, no place stated. No months named (not October/November) and no February tidy.

checks.recorded: "If practical, pick off and dispose of any leaves that remain on the plant over the winter months."
checks.page_wording: If practical, pick off and dispose of any leaves that remain on the plant over the winter months.
checks.note: Leaves remaining on roses over winter, for black spot; UK, no place stated. Page is RHS.

contradictions: Page recommends against using fungicides; no winter spray type named.

also_says.quote: Mulch is a layer of material, at least 5cm (2in) thick, applied to the soil surface in late autumn to late winter (Nov-Feb).
also_says.note: Mulching, November to February; UK, no place stated.

also_says.quote: Prune out all stem lesions in spring before leaves appear.
also_says.note: Removing black-spot stem lesions, spring; UK, no place stated; not main pruning.

checks.recorded: "Collect and destroy fallen leaves in autumn to reduce the number of overwintering resting spores"
checks.page_wording: Collect and destroy fallen leaves in autumn to reduce the number of overwintering resting spores
checks.note: Leaf clear-up in autumn, for rust control; UK, no place stated. No months named and no February tidy.

checks.recorded: "These timings reflect the typical first safe planting time in an average year."
checks.page_wording: These timings reflect the typical first safe planting time in an average year.
checks.note: About planting out tender plants (not roses), UK general. Supports the 'average year' basis; the full five-region claim needs the region list.

checks.recorded: "The Highlands and northern Scotland: mid June"
checks.page_wording: The Highlands and northern Scotland: mid June
checks.note: Fifth and last of five regions (south-west tip and south coast, southern England and south Wales, Midlands/NW England/Yorkshire/north Wales, NE England/southern Scotland/NI, Highlands). Tender plants, not roses.

checks.recorded: "Exposed, rural or higher elevation sites (e.g. Shropshire, Cotswolds, Pennines): delay 1–3 weeks"
checks.page_wording: Exposed, rural or higher elevation sites (e.g. Shropshire, Cotswolds, Pennines): delay 1-3 weeks
checks.note: Supports exposed, rural, high sites later. Page also advances sheltered/urban/coastal by 1-2 weeks and says plant later or avoid frost pockets and valley bottoms (from one fetch, not quoted). Tender plants, UK.

checks.recorded: "April 2021 recorded the most April air frosts in at least 60 years"
checks.page_wording: April 2021 recorded the most April air frosts in at least 60 years.
checks.note: Supports a late-frost example; the page also says 'Spring is variable and late frosts still occur', which carries the year-to-year point. Tender plants, UK.

checks.recorded: "A garden in a frost pocket is at significant risk of late and early frosts and has a shortened growing season"
checks.page_wording: A garden in a frost pocket is at significant risk of late and early frosts and has a shortened growing season
checks.note: Supports frost pockets being later/riskier only. Page did not clearly say sheltered, urban or coastal sites are earlier or exposed sites later (answer was NEAR, South-facing areas get more light and warmth). Not rose-specific; UK, no place stated.

sources.page_date: March 11, 2025 (published and modified in page metadata)

checks.recorded: February is the ideal month to prune hybrid tea roses
checks.page_wording: According to experienced rosarians, February is the ideal month to prune hybrid tea roses.
checks.note: Main pruning of hybrid teas in February; UK, no place stated (grower is in Norfolk). Supports February only; the finding says January and February, so this sentence covers one month of the two. Page dated March 2025.

checks.recorded: January – February: Main pruning period for hybrid tea and climbing roses before new growth begins.
checks.page_wording: January – February: Main pruning period for hybrid tea and climbing roses before new growth begins.
checks.note: Main pruning of hybrid tea and climbing roses, January to February, tied to before new growth begins; UK, no place stated. Fully supports the finding for this one grower.

checks.recorded: Autumn (October – November): Light prune tall hybrid tea roses to prevent wind damage.
checks.page_wording: Autumn (October – November): Light prune tall hybrid tea roses to prevent wind damage.
checks.note: Light autumn prune of tall hybrid teas, October to November, against wind; UK, no place stated. The finding says September to November and 'not a hard prune'; this gives October-November only, and elsewhere the page says reduce height by about 50 percent, which is large for a 'light' prune.

contradictions: Page says 'Consider a light prune in autumn, reducing their height by about 50%', much more than the 30cm of PB-CAL; qualifies 'light height reduction' in AF-9.
Page also says 'Pruning in January or February is still effective' (page wording), consistent with AF-4.

also_says.quote: February is the ideal month to prune hybrid tea roses.
also_says.note: Main pruning, February, UK no place stated (Norfolk grower)

also_says.quote: Recommends feeding in February with balanced rose fertiliser and mulch after pruning
also_says.note: Paraphrase from fetch summary, not a verified exact sentence; first feed, February, UK no place stated

also_says.quote: Summer Deadheading: Regularly remove spent flowers to encourage continuous blooming.
also_says.note: Deadheading in summer, no stop month given; UK no place stated

checks.recorded: The best time to prune your roses is during February and March.
checks.page_wording: The best time to prune your roses is during February and March.
checks.note: Main pruning of roses generally, February and March; UK, no place stated (grower in Norfolk). Supports the finding for this source. Page dated 2017, so older than the other Peter Beales pages (which say January-February).

checks.recorded: It is not recommended to hard prune them during the autumn though as the tips can then become damaged by frost.
checks.page_wording: It is not recommended to hard prune them during the autumn though as the tips can then become damaged by frost.
checks.note: Hard pruning in autumn advised against because of frost damage to tips; roses generally; UK, no place stated. Fully supports the finding.

contradictions: This 2017 page says February and March for main pruning, while the same grower's 2025 pages say January-February (PB-HT, PB-FEB); the grower's own advice differs by page.

also_says.quote: During the summer modern shrub roses require dead heading after they have flowered to help new growth develop to produce another flush later on.
also_says.note: Deadheading in summer, no stop month; UK no place stated

also_says.quote: tall Hybrid Teas that may need a slight trim to protect them from being damaged by heavy winds during the winter months
also_says.note: Autumn/winter light trim of tall hybrid teas, no month given; UK no place stated

checks.recorded: removing approximately 30cm (12 inches) from the top of established plants
checks.page_wording: Light prune remaining roses in preparation for winter months – by removing approximately 30cm (12 inches) from the top of established plants will help to protect them
checks.note: September section: light height reduction of about 30cm to protect from winter wind, explicitly not a hard prune because of frost. UK, no place stated (Norfolk grower). Supports light autumn height reduction, but only September; finding's range September to November is not covered by this page alone.

checks.recorded: Late August is usually the time you apply your last feed, to encourage the final flush
checks.page_wording: Late August is usually the time you apply your last feed, to encourage the final flush of blooms.
checks.note: August section: last feed in late August, for roses generally; UK, no place stated. Supports the finding.

checks.recorded: Traditionally, this is the best time to plant bare rooted roses
checks.page_wording: Traditionally, this is the best time to plant bare rooted roses.
checks.note: Sits in the November section, so supports November only for bare-root planting; the finding's range (October or November to March) is not covered by this sentence. UK, no place stated.

checks.recorded: This is also the time to transplant mature roses
checks.page_wording: This is also the time to transplant mature roses and replace the top two or three inches of compost.
checks.note: November section: moving established roses in November; UK, no place stated. Supports one of the stated windows (November) only.

checks.recorded: pick up any foliage that has dropped onto the soil
checks.page_wording: Remove diseased foliage from plants and pick up any foliage that has dropped onto the soil.
checks.note: The fetch placed this under OCTOBER (not November); it is about removing diseased foliage and picking up dropped leaves. Supports clearing fallen leaves in October; says nothing about November or February. UK, no place stated. Recorded fragment is only a part of the sentence.

contradictions: Calendar places first feed in March (fertiliser such as fish, blood and bone) and liquid high-potash feed from May; consistent with spring feeding but note 'Vitax Q4' is a brand and not recorded.
Calendar puts deadheading 'begins' in July; no stop date given.
Calendar gives light autumn prune in September, not October-November as in PB-HT.

also_says.quote: All established bush and repeat flowering shrubs should receive annual prune
also_says.note: February section of calendar; main pruning in February; UK no place stated (summary of fetch, wording not verified exactly)

also_says.quote: Apply a good fertiliser like Fish, Blood, and Bone
also_says.note: March section; first feed in March; UK no place stated; fetch wording not verified exactly

also_says.quote: give them added protection from frosts; once pruned the freshly cut tips are open to the winter elements and can become damaged by frost
also_says.note: September; reason for not hard pruning in autumn; UK no place stated

checks.recorded: ideally in March, as the rose starts to leave its winter, dormant state.
checks.page_wording: We recommend giving your roses a slow-release granular feed at the beginning of Spring each year, ideally in March, as the rose starts to leave its winter, dormant state.
checks.note: First feed of the year, March, tied to the rose leaving dormancy; roses generally; UK, no place stated. Supports March only; the finding's range late February to April is not covered by this sentence.

checks.recorded: after the first flush of blooms has gone over in July.
checks.page_wording: Then our Rosarians recommend giving your rose another slow-release, granular feed after the first flush of blooms has gone over in July.
checks.note: A second granular feed after the first flush, July; roses generally; UK, no place stated. Supports the finding.

checks.recorded: do your last liquid feed before the end of August
checks.page_wording: Our Rosarians advise to do your last liquid feed before the end of August and before the growth of the rose starts to slow down for autumn and winter.
checks.note: Last liquid feed before the end of August; roses generally; UK, no place stated. Note it says 'last liquid feed' (granular feeds are separate: March and July); supports the finding.

checks.recorded: prevents any new growth from being damaged by the frost.
checks.page_wording: Ending feeding at this point encourages the plant to start entering its dormant state as the weather cools and prevents any new growth from being damaged by the frost.
checks.note: Reason for stopping feeding: lets the plant enter dormancy and avoids frost damage to new growth; roses generally; UK, no place stated. Supports both parts of the finding.

also_says.quote: Stop feeding from September to February (fetch summary; not verified as an exact sentence)
also_says.note: No feeding September to February; UK no place stated; wording unverified

checks.recorded: just remember not to do anything too drastic, as it is too early to do a hard prune.
checks.page_wording: If you choose to trim your stems down, just remember not to do anything too drastic, as it is too early to do a hard prune.
checks.note: October: optional trimming of taller stems against wind, nothing drastic; roses generally; UK, no place stated (Norfolk grower). Supports 'not a hard prune' and October only; gives no amount, and the page says cut taller stems down 'to make them less vulnerable to the wind'.

checks.recorded: make sure you are still deadheading your roses, once the flowers have gone over.
checks.page_wording: As you have been throughout the summer, make sure you are still deadheading your roses, once the flowers have gone over.
checks.note: Deadheading continues in October with no stop date given; roses generally; UK, no place stated. Supports the finding.

checks.recorded: as it is too early to do a hard prune.
checks.page_wording: just remember not to do anything too drastic, as it is too early to do a hard prune.
checks.note: October: says it is too early for a hard prune, but gives no frost reason; the frost-damage reason is not on this page (it is on PB-WF and PB-CAL). UK, no place stated.

also_says.quote: you can cut your taller stems down to make them less vulnerable to the wind
also_says.note: October; taller roses, wind protection; UK no place stated

also_says.quote: remove any diseased leaves from the plant and keep an eye on it
also_says.note: October; removing diseased leaves before they fall; UK no place stated; no spray mentioned

checks.recorded: removing any fallen leaves from the ground
checks.page_wording: you can tidy them up by removing any fallen leaves from the ground and cut off any diseased leaves
checks.note: November clear-up: remove fallen leaves from the ground; roses generally; UK, no place stated (Norfolk grower). Supports November for leaf clearing; the October and February parts of the finding are not on this page.

checks.recorded: Before the winter weather takes hold, it is crucial to check the base of your roses, for root exposure.
checks.page_wording: Before the winter weather takes hold, it is crucial to check the base of your roses, for root exposure.
checks.note: November: check the base for exposed roots before winter weather; roses generally; UK, no place stated. The mulch itself is in the next sentence; this one only says check.

checks.recorded: you will need to build up a mulch layer around them to protect them from the cold.
checks.page_wording: you will need to build up a mulch layer around them to protect them from the cold.
checks.note: November: if roots are starting to show, build up a mulch layer to protect from the cold; roses generally; UK, no place stated. Mulching is conditional on roots being visible.

contradictions: Mulch is advised only if roots are starting to become visible, not as a blanket November task (qualifies AF-25).

also_says.quote: The key is to wait until the roses go into their dormant state, which usually happens when the weather is consistently 5 degrees or lower.
also_says.note: Climbers and ramblers pruning start, tied to dormancy and cold weather; UK no place stated

also_says.quote: This is usually around mid-November for most of the UK, but can be earlier in colder more northerly areas.
also_says.note: Timing of dormancy, mid-November for most of UK, earlier in colder northerly areas; bounds are vague, no named line

also_says.quote: wait until the roses go into their dormant state, which usually happens when the weather is consistently 5 degrees or lower
also_says.note: Weather and plant signal rather than date; UK no place stated

checks.recorded: December is one of the best months of the year to plant your bare root roses
checks.page_wording: December is one of the best months of the year to plant your bare root roses
checks.note: Bare-root planting in December; UK, no place stated (Norfolk grower). Supports December only; the finding's range (late autumn to March) is wider. Page says the cold ground keeps the rose dormant after planting.

also_says.quote: the ground is cold, which means the rose will stay dormant for a couple of months after it has been planted
also_says.note: December; bare-root planting; UK no place stated

checks.recorded: until the ground has thawed enough for you to plant it.

checks.note: If the ground is frozen, store the bare-root rose in water or compost and plant once thawed; roses generally; UK, no place stated. Supports the finding.

checks.recorded: January and February are the best months of the year to prune your shrubs, hybrid teas, and any other roses

checks.page_wording: February is the perfect time to tidy up your flower beds, ready for the spring.
